title: Africa’s green industrialization blind spot: who will buy?
body:
Africa’s green industrialization debate is dominated by supply: more renewables, bigger grids, new factories, critical minerals.

But the toughest question is still missing: who will buy or better still what economists call "demand"?

Consider three common scenarios:

- Scenario 1: Clean power without industry -- A country invests heavily in solar and wind. Generation capacity rises but without anchor industrial users, power demand remains weak, tariffs stay high, and clean plants are underutilized.
- Scenario 2: Green factories without markets -- A battery, fertilizer, or green cement plant is built. Inputs are available and technology is proven. But without long-term offtake agreements, the project struggles to secure finance and operate at scale.
- Scenario 3: Imports crowd out local production -- Governments talk industrialization, yet public procurement continues to favor cheaper imports. Domestic green producers are left exposed in their most fragile early years.

These outcomes are not technical failures, they are demand failures.

Green industrialization will not scale without:

- Long-term industrial offtake agreements that make investments bankable
- Anchor buyers in fertilizer, steel, cement, agro-processing, and mining
- Strategic public procurement that creates early markets for green products

Countries that industrialized successfully did not wait for demand to emerge, they created it deliberately.

If Africa wants clean power and green manufacturing to deliver jobs and competitiveness, demand creation must become a core industrial policy tool, not an afterthought.

The real question shouldn’t be all about whether Africa can produce green energy and/or manufacture low-carbon technology components. It should also be about whether it can guarantee markets for green industry.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Emmanuel Buadi Mensah Solomon Owusu Woubet Kassa, PhD
